title: “LORD, LORD!”—THE TWO WORDS THAT MAY STILL LEAVE YOU OUTSIDE HEAVEN
paragraphs: “LORD, LORD!”—THE TWO WORDS THAT MAY STILL LEAVE YOU OUTSIDE HEAVEN

They preached in His name. They performed miracles in His name. They were convinced they belonged to Him. But when they finally stood before Jesus, they heard five devastating words: “I never knew you.” What did they miss—and could we be missing the same thing?
Imagine spending your entire life believing you were going to heaven.
You prayed when life became unbearable. You sang worship songs with tears in your eyes. You shared Bible verses on Facebook. You attended church. You told people that Jesus was Lord.
Maybe you even served in ministry. Maybe people admired your faith. Maybe someone came to Christ because of something you said.
And then comes the day when everything earthly disappears.
No more Sunday services.
No more religious titles.
No more carefully maintained reputation.
No more opportunity to hide behind the version of yourself everyone else believed.
You stand before Jesus Christ.
And you are certain He will welcome you.
But then you hear something so terrifying that it makes every earthly rejection seem insignificant.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Not, “I used to know you.”
Not, “You were once Mine, but I forgot you.”
“I never knew you.”
How could someone spend years speaking about Jesus and still be a stranger to Him?
How could someone perform extraordinary works in His name and still be rejected?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
What if the greatest danger facing some professing Christians is not that they have rejected Jesus openly, but that they have mistaken religious activity for truly belonging to Him?
This is not a story invented to frighten people into religion.
These are the words of Jesus Himself.
And He spoke them while teaching people how to enter the kingdom of heaven.
In Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus declares:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Notice something that should stop us in our tracks.
These people were not denying that Jesus was Lord.
They were calling Him Lord.
Twice.
They were not claiming to have served another god.
They were appealing to what they had done in Jesus' name.
They were not presenting themselves as enemies of Christianity.
They were presenting themselves as His servants.
And yet Jesus rejected their claim to belong to Him.
Why?
Because the issue was never simply whether they knew His name.
The issue was whether they truly belonged to Him.
There is something important hidden in the original Greek that English readers can easily overlook.
When Jesus says, “Lord, Lord,” Matthew records the expression:
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, Kyrie.
Kyrie is the vocative form of kyrios, meaning “Lord,” “master,” or one who possesses authority.
The repetition creates a forceful, urgent address. These people are not casually mentioning Jesus. They are appealing to Him directly and emphatically.
But repetition does not make a confession genuine.
A person can speak the right words without surrendering to the One those words identify.
And that is precisely the contradiction Jesus exposes.
He asks elsewhere:
“Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46, KJV)
There it is.
The contradiction between confession and conduct.
Between the mouth and the heart.
Between claiming Christ's authority and refusing to submit to it.
Imagine someone standing before a king, repeatedly declaring, “Your Majesty! Your Majesty!” while deliberately rebelling against everything the king commands.
The words may acknowledge his title.
But the rebellion exposes the person's allegiance.
And Jesus is not merely an earthly king.
He is the risen Lord before whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–11).
Calling Him Lord is not a magical formula that guarantees salvation.
The question is whether our confession is the expression of genuine faith or a substitute for it.
But we must be careful here.
Because this passage has sometimes been used to terrify sincere Christians who are already struggling under the weight of guilt.
Some read these verses and immediately begin examining every failure, every temptation, every moment of weakness.
They wonder whether one more sin will cause Jesus to turn them away.
That is not the conclusion Jesus is teaching.
He is not declaring that only sinlessly perfect people enter heaven.
If that were true, nobody would enter.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
And 1 John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
The gospel does not announce that Jesus came to save people who never needed forgiveness.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
So what separates a struggling believer from the people Jesus describes?
The answer becomes clearer when we examine what these people say in their defense.
They do not cry out for mercy.
They do not appeal to Christ's sacrifice.
They do not confess their need for grace.
Instead, they present their religious achievements.
“Have we not prophesied in thy name?”
“Have we not ... cast out devils?”
“Have we not ... done many wonderful works?”
Their repeated argument is striking.
Look at what we did.
Now, the passage does not tell us everything about their inner motives. We should not pretend to know details Jesus did not reveal.
But it does show us the foundation of their appeal.
They point to extraordinary religious works as evidence that Jesus must receive them.
And Jesus exposes the fatal inadequacy of that claim.
Religious achievements, even astonishing ones, cannot establish that a person truly belongs to Christ.
A person may be publicly associated with God's work without being inwardly reconciled to God.
A person may know Christian language without possessing Christian faith.
A person may impress an audience without being approved by the Lord.
And spiritual experiences, however dramatic, must never replace the truth of God's Word as the measure of genuine discipleship.
Jesus had already warned about false prophets who appear harmless but are inwardly dangerous (Matthew 7:15–20).
He said they would be recognized by their fruits.
Then He warned that not everyone calling Him Lord would enter the kingdom.
Immediately afterward, He described two builders: one whose house stood because it rested on rock, and another whose house collapsed because it rested on sand (Matthew 7:24–27).
These teachings belong together.
The issue is not religious appearance.
It is whether a person's life rests upon Christ's words and responds to them in genuine faith.
And that brings us to another phrase in Matthew 7 that deserves our attention.
Jesus says that the one who enters the kingdom is the one who does the will of His Father.
In Greek, Matthew 7:21 uses:
ὁ ποιῶν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου
ho poiōn to thelēma tou patros mou
Meaning, “the one doing the will of My Father.”
Does that mean we earn heaven by obeying enough commandments?
No.
Scripture does not permit that conclusion.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we earn through works.
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Do you see the difference?
Good works are not the price we pay to purchase salvation. They are the fruit that genuine saving faith produces.
Obedience does not make the cross sufficient.
The cross is sufficient because Jesus is sufficient.
But when His grace truly takes hold of a life, that grace does not leave the person content to make peace with sin.
Titus 2:11–14 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace also transforms.
And Jesus Himself explains the Father's will in a way that guards us against turning salvation into a religious performance.
In John 6:40, He says:
“And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.” (KJV)
The Father's will is not separated from faith in His Son.
It begins with receiving Jesus Christ, trusting Him, and responding to His truth.
A living faith produces obedience—not perfect obedience, but a real, Spirit-enabled turning toward God.
James 2:17 tells us that faith without works is dead.
Not because works replace faith.
But because a faith that never bears fruit gives us reason to question whether it is alive.
This is where the warning becomes deeply personal.
You can attend church and still refuse to forgive someone.
You can post Scripture while privately cultivating cruelty.
You can sing about holiness while defending a secret life you have no intention of surrendering.
You can speak beautifully about God's love while repeatedly exploiting people who trust you.
You can tell the world that Jesus is Lord while treating His commands as optional whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
And perhaps nobody notices.
Your friends may not notice.
Your pastor may not notice.
Your followers may not notice.
But Jesus sees what human applause cannot reveal.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Not so that we become obsessed with appearing spiritually impressive.
But so that we stop confusing appearance with reality.
And then comes the phrase that cuts even deeper.
“I never knew you.”
The Greek reads:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
oudepote egnōn hymas
Literally, “I never knew you.”
Oudepote means “never,” or “not ever.”
Egnōn is a past-tense form of the verb ginōskō, meaning “to know.”
Of course, Jesus is not saying He lacked information about these people.
He is not an uninformed judge who failed to recognize their faces.
Throughout Scripture, God's knowledge of His people can describe something deeper than awareness of their existence.
It speaks of recognition, belonging, and relationship.
Consider 2 Timothy 2:19:
“The Lord knoweth them that are his.” (KJV)
Or John 10:14, where Jesus says:
“I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.” (KJV)
The terrifying reality in Matthew 7 is not that these people failed to make themselves famous enough for Jesus to recognize.
It is that they claimed a relationship with Him that He did not acknowledge as real.
And that changes everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about building a religious résumé.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Not merely knowing facts about Him.
Not merely knowing the songs.
Not merely knowing the vocabulary.
Not merely knowing how to sound like a believer.
But belonging to the Savior who died and rose again.
Think about Judas Iscariot.
He walked with Jesus.
He heard the teaching.
He witnessed miracles.
He was numbered among the twelve.
And yet outward proximity to Jesus did not mean his heart was faithful to Jesus.
John 12:4–6 reveals his dishonesty, and the Gospels record his betrayal.
That should make us cautious about assuming that closeness to Christian activity automatically means closeness to Christ.
But there is another disciple we must remember.
Peter.
Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ.
Peter promised loyalty.
Peter insisted he would remain faithful.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering your own voice denying the Savior you loved.
Imagine hearing the rooster and realizing that your courage had collapsed exactly as Jesus predicted.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
And yet Peter's story did not end in rejection.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Why is that so important?
Because there is a difference between falling into sin and embracing sin as your master.
There is a difference between a heart broken over failure and a heart determined to justify rebellion.
There is a difference between someone who needs restoration and someone who wants religious recognition without repentance.
Peter did not save himself by crying hard enough.
His tears were not payment for forgiveness.
His hope rested in the Savior who had prayed for him, died for sinners, risen from the grave, and graciously restored him.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
Maybe you have failed Jesus.
Maybe you have been hiding a habit you are ashamed to name.
Maybe you have promised God you would change, only to find yourself fighting the same temptation again.
Maybe your faith feels weak.
Maybe your prayers have become painfully honest because you no longer have the strength to pretend.
Do not mistake the warning of Matthew 7 for a declaration that every struggling Christian is beyond hope.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV)
Those words matter.
The same Jesus who warns against false assurance promises to receive those who truly come to Him.
He does not turn away repentant sinners because their past is ugly.
He does not require you to clean yourself into worthiness before receiving His grace.
He calls you to come.
To believe.
To repent.
To follow Him.
And when you fall, to return to Him rather than making peace with the darkness.
First John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing to those who confess their sins.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The answer to false assurance is not endless self-torment. It is genuine faith in the genuine Savior.
Still, there is one final Greek expression in Jesus' warning that we cannot ignore.
When He says, “Depart from me, ye that work iniquity,” Matthew records:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν
hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian
Meaning, “you who practice lawlessness.”
The word anomia carries the sense of lawlessness, wrongdoing, or disregard for God's law.
This is not simply a description of people who have ever sinned.
That would describe all humanity.
Jesus identifies them as practitioners of lawlessness—people whose religious claims coexist with a life characterized by disregard for God's will.
Their profession and their practice contradict one another.
And that contradiction exposes the emptiness of their claim.
Notice also that Jesus does not say, “You did not perform enough miracles.”
He does not say, “You failed to become influential enough.”
He does not say, “Your ministry was too small.”
He does not demand a larger audience, a more impressive title, or a more successful religious career.
He exposes lawlessness and denies that they truly belonged to Him.

Which means someone serving quietly, loving faithfully, repenting sincerely, and trusting Christ may possess something infinitely more valuable than the most admired religious personality in the world.
The approval of Jesus is worth more than the applause of millions.
And now we need to ask a question that modern Christianity cannot afford to avoid.
What happens when we turn following Jesus into a performance?
When we measure spiritual success only by views, followers, donations, applause, or public recognition?
When being seen as holy becomes more important than actually pursuing holiness?
When defending our reputation becomes more urgent than confessing our sin?
When we are more concerned about losing an audience than grieving the heart of God?
We may build something impressive in the eyes of people while neglecting what matters most before Christ.
And those of us involved in Christian ministry must take this warning seriously.
No platform is a substitute for prayer.
No viral message is a substitute for obedience.
No ministry income is proof of God's approval.
Even sharing the gospel publicly cannot replace personally trusting the gospel we proclaim.
This warning belongs to the preacher as much as the listener.
To the writer as much as the reader.
To the person behind the microphone as much as the person sitting in the last pew.
It belongs to all of us.
And perhaps that is why Jesus spoke it so plainly.
Not to entertain our curiosity about who might be rejected.
But to confront our tendency to build confidence on everything except Him.
There is a danger in reading Matthew 7 and immediately thinking of someone else.
That hypocritical pastor.
That judgmental relative.
That Christian who hurt you.
That person who posts Bible verses but treats others terribly.
Perhaps some of those concerns are legitimate.
But Jesus did not give us this warning so that we could spend the rest of our lives confidently assigning other people to hell.
Only God knows the heart perfectly.
The warning calls us first to examine ourselves.
Second Corinthians 13:5 says:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” (KJV)
So perhaps the question today is not, “Which Christian do I think Jesus will reject?”
Perhaps it is...
“Lord, have I mistaken familiarity with Christianity for surrender to You?”
“Have I been using Your name while resisting Your Word?”
“Have I been defending a sin that You are calling me to confess?”
“Have I been trusting my religious accomplishments more than Your finished work?”
“Am I following You because I love You, or merely because I want what You can give me?”
Those questions are uncomfortable.
But discomfort can become mercy when it leads us toward repentance.
The worst response to Jesus' warning would be to hear it, feel briefly frightened, and then return unchanged to the very life He is calling us to leave.
The better response is to bring our hearts into the light.
Not with theatrical promises.
Not with a performance designed to impress others.
But with honesty before God.
“Lord Jesus, I cannot save myself.
I have sinned against You.
I have sometimes loved the appearance of faith more than the cost of following You.
Forgive me.
Expose what I have hidden.
Teach me to trust You, obey You, and love what You love.
Do not let me settle for a religious reputation while neglecting a real relationship with You.
Change my heart by Your grace.
I belong to You, not because I am worthy, but because You are the Savior of sinners.”
If that prayer expresses your heart, remember that the power is not in repeating a particular set of words.
The power belongs to Jesus Christ, who saves those who come to Him in faith.
And that leads us to the greatest hope in this entire passage.
The warning is terrifying.
But the gospel is glorious.
Because the same Jesus who will one day judge the world is the Jesus who willingly went to the cross to rescue sinners.
He did not merely tell us to become better people.
He bore our sins.
He suffered for the unrighteous.
He died and rose again.
First Peter 3:18 declares:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” (KJV)
Think about those final words.
That He might bring us to God.
Not merely bring us into a religious organization.
Not merely bring us into a social circle.
Not merely bring us into a lifestyle that looks respectable.
Bring us to God.
The very relationship sin had broken is what Christ came to restore.
The separation we could never overcome by our own goodness is what His sacrifice addresses.
The judgment we deserve is why His grace is so astonishing.
And the resurrection assures us that the crucified Savior is alive.
That is why the answer to Matthew 7 is not to work frantically until we feel worthy of heaven.
It is to abandon every false refuge and trust the One who alone can save.
True faith is not opposed to obedience.
True faith leads us into obedience.
True grace is not permission to cherish sin.
True grace teaches us to turn from it.
True discipleship is not pretending we never stumble.
It is following Jesus with a heart that continually returns to Him in repentance and faith.
And when we understand that, something beautiful happens.
We stop asking only, “How much can I do for Jesus so He will accept me?”
And begin asking, “Because Jesus has shown such mercy to me, how can I live for His glory?”
That is where generosity finds its proper place.
That is where service becomes worship rather than self-promotion.
That is where sharing the gospel becomes an act of love rather than a quest for attention.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a platform that replaces your local church.
Not to sell salvation.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, searching, and growing people back to Jesus Christ and the truth of Scripture.
If this message has helped you confront something you were avoiding, consider what might happen if it reaches someone who has quietly confused church attendance with salvation.
Someone who has spent years pretending.
Someone who believes their past is too shameful for forgiveness.
Someone who is slowly walking away from Christ because they have mistaken human hypocrisy for the character of Jesus.
Not merely because it might reach thousands.
But because it might reach the one person who needs it.
And if this message has exposed something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend otherwise.
If God has been restoring you after a season of wandering, share your testimony if you feel comfortable.
Your honesty may encourage another believer who thought they were the only one struggling.
There is room here for serious questions, honest struggles, biblical encouragement, and a deeper pursuit of Christ.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible.
And if this ministry has become a meaningful part of your spiritual growth, I want to invite you into something more personal.
For some, a message like this may be the beginning of a difficult but life-changing conversation with God.
For others, it may be a reminder to return to the Savior they have neglected.
For still others, it may be the encouragement they need to keep walking faithfully.
It is an opportunity to give generously toward a ministry you believe is serving Christ faithfully.
You are no less welcome.
You are no less valuable.
And your ability to give money has absolutely nothing to do with whether Jesus loves you or receives you.
Every act of genuine service matters when it is offered to God in faith and love.
Because one day, Gospel Warrior will not be the name that matters most.
Our books will not matter most.
Our most widely shared articles will not matter most.
The question will not be whether you followed a Christian page.
It will not be whether you purchased a Christian product.
It will not be whether you supported a ministry financially.
The question raised by Matthew 7 is far more searching.
Do you truly belong to Jesus Christ?
Have you trusted Him as Savior and acknowledged Him as Lord?
Is your life being shaped by His grace, His truth, and His call to repentance?
And here is the hope that should never be lost beneath the weight of this warning.
Jesus did not speak these words so that we would admire the danger from a distance.
He spoke them while people could still hear, repent, believe, and build their lives upon His words.
Today, you are hearing His warning.
Today, the invitation of the gospel is still being proclaimed.
Today, you can turn from empty religious confidence and come to the Savior who receives sinners.
You do not need a spotless history to come to Jesus.
You need the Savior whose blood cleanses sinners.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive spiritual résumé.
You need to trust the crucified and risen Lord.
You do not need to pretend your wounds, failures, and sins never happened.
You need to bring them into the light of His grace.
That is the heart of our message.
From rebellion to repentance.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual death to new life in Christ.
Not because we rewrote our own stories.
But because Jesus is the Redeemer who changes everything.
And when you finally stand before Him, may your confidence never be the number of things you accomplished while saying His name.
May your confidence be Jesus Christ Himself—the Savior who died for sinners, rose victorious, and knows those who are His.
Because the most frightening possibility is not that the world might forget your name.
It is that you could spend your life making the name of Jesus part of your public identity while never truly surrendering your heart to Him.
And the most beautiful possibility?
That the very Savior who warns you today is also the Savior who invites you to come to Him and live.
Do not settle for being recognized as someone who speaks about Jesus when His grace is inviting you to become someone who truly belongs to Him.
